Here's where it stands. ## The design that falls out of your three bullets **Layer 1 — connectivity (island → island).** Built from FollowMe, not from a timetable: per device, collapse consecutive stationary polls into *stay points*, then every move between two stays is a directed trip with an observed duration. Snapped to the 1,134 island polygons, that gives **20,960 observed crossings → 5,789 directed edges → 4,132 island pairs**, median crossing 0.86 h at 7 kn. `data/derived/sea_edges.csv` **Layer 2 — key services.** I dropped the school-website scrape (grade range was only parseable for 70 of 220 schools) and parsed MoE *School Statistics 2024* pp. 22–37 instead: one row per island, 16 grade columns × M/F. **It reconciles exactly — grade 11–12 = 5,105 students, matching the published national figure to the student.** 44 islands teach grade 11–12, 181 teach grade 7–10. **Layer 3 — \"can I get from A to B\".** Floyd–Warshall over the island graph, edge = observed median crossing, 1 h transfer, budgeted at 2 sailings so a 4-boat journey reports *not accessible* instead of a fake 40-hour number. ``` $ python scripts/query_access.py --from Baarah --atoll \"Haa Alifu\" Baarah (Haa Alifu) — population 1,141, children 0-17 406 nearest grade 11-12 school : 2.17 h (130 min) islands reachable : 715 $ python scripts/query_access.py --from \"Malé\" --to Kulhudhuffushi Malé City -> Kulhudhuffushi: 8.47 h, 3 sailings ``` ## What the numbers already say | measure | value | |---|---| | inhabited islands / residents | 187 / 448,819 (87 % of the 515,132 Census total) | | can reach grade 11–12 within 2 h | 156 islands, **420,175 people** | | within 4 h | 181 islands, 443,519 people | | no reachable post-16 school | 2 islands, 1,115 people — both have *zero observed boat traffic*, so it's a data gap, not a proven cut-off | | higher-secondary net enrolment | **29.9 %** (M 25.8 / F 34.3) vs primary 91.9 % | **This reframes your pitch, and you should let it.** \"Islands lack transport links to schools\" is not defensible — 44 islands teach A-level and 156 are within 2 h. What *is* defensible: (a) the 27 islands outside 2 h, (b) **Malé→Kulhudhuffushi is 8.5 h and 3 sailings by sea but ~50 min by air** — so the multi-modal choice is the finding, not the decoration, and (c) the NER collapse at grade 11: the barrier isn't the daily trip, it's that post-16 means *leaving home*, and only 30 % do. ## Three things still open 1. **Air layer** — the biggest distortion right now; sea-only timings overstate the barrier by a factor of 10 on northern routes. 14 domestic airports → Velana, block time + 1 h transfer, re-run. ~45 min, highest marginal value left. 2. **Fares** — your card says \"affordable\" and there is no fare data anywhere in the folder; only Avas taxi zones (MVR 30–120). If teams finish with the same total, the team with the higher average of Impact plus Scalability ranks first, then the team with the higher Technical execution score, and then the judges vote","assistantReply":"Built and running at **http://127.0.0.1:8010** (run it yourself with `cd web && python3 manage.py runserver 8000`). ![Island access explorer](docs/app-desktop.png) ## Django + HTMX was the right call Not because it's fashionable, but because this app is **four HTMX fragments over read-only CSVs** — and that's exactly the shape Django is good at, with none of the cost: - **No models, no migrations, no database.** `DATABASES = {}`. The whole dataset is 187 islands + 8,274 edges, loaded once into memory by `web/access/data.py`. A DB here would be ceremony. - **Server-rendered fragments, no JS framework.** Every interaction swaps an HTML partial: `/island/<id>/` → the profile card, `/route/?from=&to=` → the journey, `/ranked/?atoll=&band=` → the table. The first paint and every click after it go through the same template. - **Dijkstra in Python, rendered in HTML.** The route view shows the actual legs — *Kulhudhuffushi → Funadhoo 1.94 h → Malé City 4.74 h, 7.68 h total, 2 sailings, 1 h of that waiting for a connection*. - **Vendored, offline-safe.** htmx, Leaflet and the CSS are local files (no CDN); the map is `circleMarker`s over a CSS sea gradient, no tile server. Venue wifi can die and the demo still works. ## The one thing I'd flag The model's honesty is now visible in the UI, and that's deliberate: three capital routes (**Addu, Fuvahmulah, Thinadhoo → Malé**) return *\"no observed journey within two sailings\"*. That's real — those islands have no observed sea link to the capital in the August GPS — and it's the strongest argument for the **air layer**, which is still unbuilt. Adding 14 domestic airports to the graph would turn those three red islands green and probably change your headline number. Worth 45 minutes before the slides. ## What I fixed along the way Three bugs that would have looked bad on a projector: 1. **`r.name` returned the node ID.** In pandas, a Series' `.name` is its index label, not the `name` column — so the profile card and route legs showed `MV002012` instead of `Kulhudhuffushi`. 2. **The graph only had 724 edges.** The first version filtered edges to the 187 inhabited islands, which deleted every transfer through an uninhabited airport or resort island, and broke Addu entirely. Now 8,274. 3. **The map was invisible.** 186 island polygons at national zoom are sub-pixel slivers, and OSM tiles failed offline. Replaced with population-scaled circles on a sea gradient. Also: the whole repo is now under git (68 files, 36 MB; the 1.8 GB GPS is gitignored), `requirements.txt` and a README with sources, run steps and an AI-assistance note are in place, and the tablet layout collapses to one column. Want me to do the **air layer** next, or add the fares page so \"affordable\" in your challenge card has evidence behind it?","parentTurnId":"dialogue:15ti78t:0004","jumped":false,"relatedNodeIds":[],"createdAt":1792820388161,"updatedAt":1792820951224,"title":"Datathon 2026 - Judging Crite…","summary":"Built and running at **http://127.0.0.1:8010** (run it yourself with `cd web && python3 manage.py runserver 8000`). ![Island access explorer](docs/app-desktop.png) ## Django + HTMX was the right call…","lastSeenAt":1792820951224}

Three things in this rubric change what we should do, so I re-scored us against it. ## What the rubric actually rewards **The 1–5 scale means partial credit is expensive.** `score/5 × weight × 100` — dropping from 4 to 3 on Technical execution costs 4 points; dropping 4 to 3 on Impact costs 3 *and* loses the first tie-break. **Two sentences are aimed squarely at what we built:** - *\"A platform, app or dashboard is not innovative on its own.\"* Our innovation is the **method** — a network reconstructed from 17.4 M GPS points instead of copied from a timetable. If slide 2 leads with \"we built a Django dashboard\", a judge scores Innovation 2 and that is 4 points gone. The app is the demo surface, never the pitch. - *Data Utilization now names the allowed sources.* We're compliant — 4 organiser datasets + 3 public official sources — but **FollowMe carries the entire model** while MTCC, MACL and Avas sit as context. That's the weakest link in a 15 % criterion. ## Honest self-assessment: ~76 / 100 today | Criterion | Weight | Now | Points | Biggest gap | |---|---|---|---|---| | Relevance | 10 % | 5 | 10.0 | — | | Data Utilization | 15 % | 4 | 12.0 | FollowMe does the work; nothing cross-checks it | | Innovation | 10 % | 4 | 8.0 | the method isn't *named* as the innovation yet | | **Technical execution** | **20 %** | 4 | 16.0 | 3 capital routes read as broken (they're the air gap) | | **Impact** | **15 %** | 3 | 9.0 | **no named decision-maker, no decision output** | | **Scalability** | **15 %** | 3 | 9.0 | refresh path asserted, never demonstrated | | Clarity | 5 % | 4 | 4.0 | slides not built | | Teamwork | 10 % | 4 | 8.0 | needs two+ speakers, visible roles | **Impact and Scalability are both 15 % *and* both tie-breakers — they're the cheapest 12 points on the board,** and they're exactly what we've invested least in. ## The five actions, in points order 1. **Name the user and ship one decision** (Impact, 15 %): the **Planning & Research Division at MoE** — the unit that publishes the very statistics we parse — plus MTCC/RTL scheduling. Output: the 27 islands beyond 2 h with population, children, hours, and *the specific link whose addition would fix each*. 2. **Prove the refresh** (Scalability, 15 %): `make refresh GPS=<next month>` and show it run on a one-week subset, so data-sensitivity is demonstrated rather than claimed. 3. **Air layer** (Technical, 20 %): 14 domestic airports; kills the three false \"unreachable\" routes before a judge clicks them. 4. **Cross-validate FollowMe against MTCC** (Data, 15 %): MTCC reports ridership on 8 ferry routes; we observe crossings on those same routes. If the two agree, we've used two organiser datasets to check each other — the best possible answer to \"is the data used correctly?\" 5. **8-slide story with the method as hero** (Clarity + Innovation). My recommendation: **1 and 4 next, then 3.** They're worth the most points, they're mostly data work we already have loaded, and they convert the project from \"impressive map\" into \"a decision someone can act on\" — which is what 4 and 5 on Impact actually looks like. metadata.record: {"id":"dialogue:15ti78t:0007","sessionId":"dialogue-session:15ti78t","seq":7,"userQuery":"make sure anythig we do follows the Judging criteria","assistantReply":"Agreed — so I turned the rubric into an enforceable rule and then spent this turn moving the three criteria that carry 50 of the 100 points. **The rule, written down:** [docs/criteria-map.md](docs/criteria-map.md) — every artifact must name the criterion it earns, plus an explicit list of what we *refuse* to build because it moves none (no login, no database, no fares page without fare data, no second dashboard — several of those would actively cost Innovation points). ## Impact 15 % (also tie-break #1) — built [docs/findings.md](docs/findings.md) + `data/derived/priority_gaps.csv` + a new panel in the app: ![Priority gaps](docs/app-desktop.png) **28 islands, 21,281 residents, 6,758 children** cannot reach grade 11–12 within two hours. Each row names the school island it is nearest to and prices a direct link. The finding that matters for a real decision: > **Gan (Laamu, 4,815 people, 1,457 children) is 9.3 km from Fonadhoo, which teaches grade 11–12 — and still takes 2.16 h** because the connection runs the wrong way round the atoll. That's a scheduling fix, not a capital project. Named user: **MoE Planning & Research Division** — the unit that publishes the statistics we parse — plus MTCC route planning. Named action: rank boarding/subsidy spend by children, not by island. ## Scalability 15 % (tie-break #1) — built - `make refresh GPS=<new month>` rebuilds the whole model. - `make check` asserts **13 published numbers** (5,105 students in grades 11–12, 187 islands, 159 within 2 h, 427,538 residents, 28 gaps, …) and fails loudly if one drifts. - I switched the Makefile to the default `python3` and had to `pip install openpyxl` into it — so `make` now genuinely works end to end on a clean interpreter, which was not true an hour ago. ## Technical 20 % — a real bug fixed, which changed the numbers While building the gap table I found the analysis script was counting **causeway legs as sailings**. Feydhoo (Addu) was being reported as **2.45 h** from a school that is a 25-minute drive away, because its road chain consumed the two-sailing budget. Fixed by contracting road components into single graph nodes with per-island road offsets — the same semantics the web app already used.
